summaries.example: Imagine a door that is closed now. One question is, “Can it open later?” Another is, “Could it have been open at this exact moment?” Medieval thinkers noticed that these questions are different. Some said a present fact becomes fixed when it happens. Others argued that another way things could have been may still count as possible at the same time.
summaries.summary: Medieval philosophers asked what words such as “possible,” “necessary,” and “impossible” mean. Ancient views often linked possibility to what happens sometimes, to a thing’s powers, or to what can be imagined without contradiction. Early medieval writers, using works by Aristotle and Boethius, continued these approaches. Christian thinkers also discussed a different picture: God could choose among alternative histories. In the thirteenth century, many logicians connected necessity with the essential nature of things. In the fourteenth century, Duns Scotus gave special importance to alternatives that could exist at the same time. Ockham and Buridan then built more systematic logical theories, separating different ways a sentence can say that something is possible or necessary.
key_ideas: Ancient philosophers used several ideas of possibility, including powers, what happens sometimes, and what does not create a contradiction.
Early medieval thinkers learned much from ancient writers, especially through Boethius.
Some medieval theologians connected possibility with God choosing among different ways history could have gone.
In the fourteenth century, thinkers such as Duns Scotus, Ockham, and Buridan developed more detailed accounts of possibility and necessity.
summaries.why_it_matters: These questions help us understand how people reason about choices, change, rules, and what could have happened. They also show that the meaning of a simple word like “can” depends on the question being asked. Studying medieval ideas helps explain the long history behind modern discussions of possibility and necessity.

important_terms.definition: A way of talking about whether something must happen, can happen, or cannot happen.
Something that can happen, even if it does not happen.
Something that must be true or must happen.
A real power or ability that can bring about an action or change.
The idea that different things could happen at the same moment, even though only one happens in our history.

questions_to_think_about: Is something possible only if it really happens someday?
Can an event be fixed now but still have been avoidable earlier?
What is the difference between having the power to do something and actually doing it?
Can two different things be possible even when only one becomes real?

summaries.example: Consider the statement, “A person who is standing can sit.” On one reading, it says that the person can be both standing and sitting in the same situation, which is false. On another reading, it says that the standing person has the ability to sit, perhaps at a later time, which is true. Medieval logicians called these de dicto and de re readings. Later thinkers also asked whether the second possibility could remain open at the very moment when the person is standing.
summaries.summary: The SEP entry traces changing accounts of modality from ancient philosophy through the fourteenth century. Ancient thinkers employed several paradigms: a frequency model, according to which possibility is associated with what occurs at least sometimes; a potency model based on capacities for change; diachronic accounts of alternatives relative to a time; and a non-contradiction model. These approaches usually concerned one actual history and did not preserve simultaneous alternatives. Boethius transmitted and adapted them for medieval readers, especially in debates about future contingents and the necessity of the present. Augustine’s theological picture of divine choice helped introduce a different framework in which alternative histories could be considered together. Thirteenth-century logical treatises analyzed modal sentences through distinctions such as de dicto and de re, and often treated modality as grounded in essential structures of things. Duns Scotus made simultaneous alternatives central to contingency, while Ockham and Buridan rejected many essentialist assumptions and developed more differentiated systems of modal logic.
key_ideas: Ancient paradigms interpreted modality through frequency, potency, temporal alternatives, or non-contradictory actualization; they generally did not use simultaneous alternatives.
Boethius preserved several Aristotelian approaches while also discussing future contingents, free choice, and the distinction between present necessity and earlier openness.
Twelfth-century theological discussions, influenced by Augustine, treated divine choice among alternative histories as a foundation for a newer modal framework.
Thirteenth-century Latin logicians often interpreted Aristotelian modal syllogisms through essentialist distinctions, including necessary predication per se and accidental necessity.
Duns Scotus defined contingency through the possibility of an opposite at the very time an event occurs, challenging the traditional necessity of the present.
Fourteenth-century authors increasingly separated de dicto and de re modalities and developed more systematic modal logic, especially in the work of Ockham and Buridan.
summaries.why_it_matters: The history of medieval modality shows that debates about “could,” “must,” and “cannot” involve both language and metaphysics. A modal claim may concern a sentence, a thing’s power, a time, an essential nature, or a range of alternative states of affairs. Medieval disagreements therefore anticipate issues in contemporary modal logic while also reflecting distinct views about nature, causation, freedom, divine knowledge, and the structure of reality.

important_terms.definition: The philosophical study of necessity, possibility, impossibility, and contingency.
A claim or state of affairs that could be true or actual, without necessarily being so.
A claim or state of affairs that cannot fail to be true or actual in the relevant sense.
A possibility understood as a real capacity, tendency, or power to act or change.
A possibility involving alternatives across time, such as what could happen later from an earlier moment.
A theory in which possibility and contingency involve alternatives available at the same time.
A reading that places the modal qualification on a whole proposition, as in “That the person sits is possible.”
A reading that attributes possibility or necessity to a thing or subject, as in “The standing person can sit.”

questions_to_think_about: Does the fact that an event is occurring now make it necessary, or only temporarily fixed?
Should a possibility require a real power, or is freedom from contradiction enough?
Why might the sentence “A standing person can sit” have both a true and a false interpretation?
Are natural regularities logically necessary, or could they be stable patterns that might be overridden?
What does a theory of modality gain by distinguishing propositions about actual things from propositions about possible beings?

summaries.example: Suppose your school play is tomorrow. Today, you can still choose whether to speak loudly or softly. Once the play is happening, your words at that moment are fixed: you are speaking loudly or softly. Medieval philosophers asked whether this means the present is necessary, or whether the other choice remains possible in some sense at that same time. Their answers depended on whether they were talking about a future opportunity, a present fact, or an alternative situation.
summaries.summary: Medieval theories of modality study the meanings of possibility, necessity, impossibility, and contingency. The entry begins with ancient approaches. Some treated possibility as what occurs sometimes, necessity as what always occurs, and impossibility as what never occurs. Others explained possibility through powers or through an assumption that leads to no contradiction. Another approach considered alternatives from an earlier time, while generally allowing them to disappear once the future became fixed. Boethius transmitted these ideas and applied them to questions about future contingents and free choice. Medieval theology, especially the Augustinian idea of divine choice, helped develop a model of alternative histories existing as options. In thirteenth-century logic, writers analyzed modal sentences and syllogisms using distinctions between essential and accidental necessity and between de dicto and de re readings. Duns Scotus emphasized alternatives at the same time as an event. Later fourteenth-century logicians criticized older essentialist models and developed more complete accounts of modal propositions and logical consequences.
key_ideas: Ancient philosophers did not use one single theory of modality. They connected possibility with repeated occurrence, natural powers, future alternatives, or freedom from contradiction.
Boethius combined inherited ancient ideas with discussions of free choice, chance, and whether future statements are already true or false.
In the twelfth century, theological debates encouraged a model in which different histories could be possible because God could choose among them.
Many thirteenth-century logicians understood modal logic through the essential properties of things and carefully examined how modal statements change when their wording changes.
Duns Scotus argued that a contingent event could have had an opposite outcome at the very same time, not merely at an earlier time.
Fourteenth-century thinkers, especially Ockham and Buridan, made modal logic more systematic by separating several kinds of de dicto and de re claims.
summaries.why_it_matters: Modal reasoning appears whenever people ask whether something had to happen, could have happened differently, or is impossible. Medieval philosophers showed that these questions can concern time, causation, language, natural powers, or alternative situations. Their work also helped shape later studies of modal logic, conditionals, freedom, knowledge, and possible worlds.

important_terms.definition: A philosophical word for different ways something may be: required, allowed, ruled out, or neither required nor ruled out.
What may happen or be true, even if it does not actually happen.
What must happen or be true, given the relevant conditions.
A capacity or power that makes an action or change possible.
Possibilities considered from an earlier time, before it is settled which outcome will occur.
Different possible outcomes considered as available at one time.
The view that a modal phrase describes a whole statement, such as “It is necessary that the door is closed.”
The view that a modal phrase describes a thing or subject, such as “The closed door can open.”

questions_to_think_about: If something happens now, does that show it had to happen?
Can a thing have the power to do something even when outside conditions prevent it?
Why can one sentence about a standing person’s ability to sit be understood in two ways?
Should “possible” mean “not contradictory,” or should it require a real power?
How might beliefs about divine knowledge affect ideas about future choices?
